 A. Adequacy of Application

       Oncor and LCRA recommended 122 alternative routes for the Commission to take into

consideration in determining the best meets route for the Project. These 122 alternative routes are

not an adequate number of reasonably differentiated routes to allow the Commission to conduct a

proper evaluation. Three parties, Save the Lampasas, 4K Land and Cattle Company, and the

Burnet County Commissioners Court filed challenges demonstrating severe infirmities with the

routing analysis prepared by the Applicants, including a lack of geographically diverse alternatives

which resulted in an unfair concentration of proposed alternative routes

       Specifically, there are two areas where there are less than five east-west route links (or

“corridors”) whereas the remaining portions of the study area have five corridors or more.13 This

includes the far western end of the project (Links P1, R1, and R2) and towards the eastern portion

of the study area in Burnet County (Links G51, G6, and G44). At the Hearing on the Merits, Oncor

and LCRA Witness, Ms. Brenda J. Perkins, testified that Applicants evaluated five corridors, yet

these two areas only have three corridors or routing links.14 The deficiency in route link options

creates an unfair bias towards those links and the links that feed into them thus severely limiting

the options available to the Commission. This causes particular links to be critical to most

alternative routes, and as a result, those links may be selected not based on the evaluation of the

factors laid out by the Public Utility Regulatory Act or Commission Rules but solely because that

link is relied upon by a disproportionate number of alternative routes.

eastern portion of the study area (Links G51, G6, and G44) has caused a majority of the alternative

 B. Habitable Structures

       One of the key factors in evaluating the certification and routing of a transmission project

is the impact on habitable structures and whether the route conforms with the Commission’s policy

of “prudent avoidance.”18 “Prudent avoidance” is defined as “[t]he limiting of exposures to electric

and magnetic fields that can be avoided with reasonable investments of money and effort.”19 A

critical factor taken into account for accomplishing the goal of prudent avoidance is limiting the

number of habitable structures within close proximity to the proposed transmission line. A

habitable structure is a structure “normally inhabited by humans or intended to be inhabited by

humans on a daily or regular basis.”20 Habitable structures include single-family and multi-family

dwellings, mobile homes, apartment buildings, commercial and industrial structures, business

structures, churches, hospitals, nursing homes, and schools.21

       The habitable structure counts for routes that use Link G13 range from 80 to 179 and routes

that use Link G9 range from 136 to 184.22 The habitable structure count for routes that do not use

Links G9 or G13 range from 104 to 157.23 The habitable structure counts stem from the

requirement in the Commission Rule that includes as a factor in selecting a route, “owners of land

that contains a habitable structure . . . within 500 feet of the centerline of a transmission project

greater than 230 kV . . . .”24 This standard was created before 765 kV transmission lines were built

 III.   EVIDENCE SUPPORTS SELECTION OF ROUTE 296 AS THE BEST MEETS
                                ROUTE

       As explained in detail above, Links G9 and G13 are inferior links under the Commission’s

routing criteria and should not be used in an approved transmission line connecting Bell County

East Switch to Big Hill Substation. The Applicants’ proposed best meets route, Route 894, and

Commission Staff’s proposed best meets route, Route 487, should therefore not be selected.

Instead, Route 296 should be selected as the best meets route. With respect to the objective criteria

set forth in PURA and the Commission Rules, Route 296 performs as well as or better than Routes

487 or 894. Specifically, Route 296 runs less than two miles longer than Routes 894 or 487. Route

296 is approximately 0.61 miles longer than Route 894. The cost of the most expensive route is

$1,857,768,000 and the cost of the least expensive route is $1,636,232,000.53 This is only

$221,536,000 apart. The cost of Route 29654 is a 1% difference from Routes 89455 or 48756.

Applicants’ witness, Corin Cooley, confirmed at the hearing that in estimating costs for the

proposed transmission routes, Applicants included a 10-15% contingency in the cost estimates.57

Although one route may be a small percentage more expensive than another, once the transmission

line is actually built, that route could be less expensive than the originally estimated cost versus

the other route that was estimated to be less expensive. This furthers the argument that although

Routes 894 or 487 outperform Route 296 when it comes to cost, this is by a mere 1% and should

not be a determinative factor in deciding Routes 894 or 487 better meet the Commission’s criteria.
